subject: Accounting
title: Window Dressing
description: A fast breakdown of Window Dressing for builders.

hook.text: Just before quarter end, a company repays a loan—then borrows it right back. Why?

buildup.text: Window dressing makes financial statements look better at reporting dates.

discovery.text: Companies time transactions to improve ratios, reduce visible debt, or inflate cash balances.

twist.text: It's often legal but misleading. The company on December 31 isn't the same one on January 2.

climax.text: Experienced analysts compare multiple quarters to see through temporary cosmetic fixes.

quiz.question: What is window dressing in accounting?
options: Timing transactions to improve reported numbers

details.summary: Window dressing is the practice of making financial statements look better than reality right before a reporting date—through timing of transactions, short-term borrowing, or delaying payments. This topic explains common techniques and how to see through them.
details.whyItMatters: Window dressing is the gray area between legitimate timing decisions and outright fraud. Recognizing these techniques prevents investors from being misled by temporarily improved numbers.
takeaways: Common techniques include delaying purchases, accelerating collections, and short-term borrowing before period-end
Lehman Brothers' Repo 105 was an extreme example of window dressing that crossed into deception
Comparing quarter-end balances to mid-quarter averages can reveal window dressing patterns

faq.question: What is window dressing in financial statements?
faq.answer: Window dressing involves timing transactions to make financial statements look better at the reporting date. Examples include collecting receivables aggressively before quarter-end, taking short-term loans to boost cash balances, or delaying purchases until after the reporting date.

faq.question: How can investors detect window dressing?
faq.answer: Compare quarter-end figures to quarterly averages disclosed in footnotes or estimated from daily data. Watch for unusual cash balance jumps at period-end that reverse quickly. Look for spikes in short-term borrowing near quarter-end. Check if receivables and payables have unusual timing patterns.
